premises.declaration: SPEC §14's boundary rule (SPEC.md:2781-2789): the trust boundary encloses the protection domains the Tenant controls, and a third party is not one of them. premises.owed: The seam carries no idempotency key, so the claim that a repeated completion is a second inference rather than a deduplicated one is a claim about the endpoint. Discharging it needs a live lane against a real endpoint that sends the same body twice and observes two distinct completions and two charges. Until then the runtime's replay safety rests on the kernel's content-addressed reply and reconstructed request, not on the provider.

The contract observes that an aborted call answers abandoned rather than a refusal; it cannot observe that the endpoint stopped generating. Discharging it needs a live lane that aborts a real in-flight completion and reads the provider's own accounting for the abandoned request.

premises.owed: The service is declared and entirely unbound. `implements WebTransport` occurs nowhere in any package's src, and `new WebBackend` occurs only in test/profiles/facets/web.test.ts, so no src module constructs the backend or the facet either. Both contract runs are therefore references, distinguished by which of the two provider obligations each discharges. Discharging this needs a WebTransport implementation in some package's src plus a src composition site that builds a WebBackend with it; the contract body then takes it as a third implementation with no change to the suite, and this service's adapter list stops reading "absent".

Four of the five collaborators WebBackend takes have no implementation anywhere in src: WebUrlPolicy, WebCallerHeaderPolicy, WebCredentialPolicy and WebResponseCache (only FixedWindowRatePolicy exists). So the allowlist and SSRF decision P11-WEB-URL-SAFETY rests on is made by no code in this repository; the facet enforces that the question was asked and that the answer was well shaped. Discharging this needs a WebUrlPolicy that actually resolves targets, and adversarial cases against it: a link-local metadata address, loopback in decimal and hexadecimal forms, an IPv6 loopback, a hostname resolving into a private range, and a redirect from a public host to a private one. None of it is assertable today because there is nothing to assert it against.

WebTransport's docstring obligation is discharged by a provider's own local ledger. WebTransportRequest carries the authorization, method, headers and body, and the EffectDispatch arrives as a separate argument, so the protocol never says how the idempotency key reaches the remote service: no header placement, no declared field. A provider can honour the letter of the obligation and still cause a duplicate effect at the far end after a crash. Discharging this needs either a declared wire placement for the key in WebTransportRequest, or live evidence from a real provider that a replayed request under one key is deduplicated remotely. Neither is reachable in any local lane.

Neither WebBackend.fetch nor WebTransport.send takes an AbortSignal, so a caller's own withdrawal is not observable in this reply vocabulary at all — which is why this contract has no abandoned kind while model.inference does, and why a cancelled Turn's in-flight egress request has no defined outcome here. Discharging this needs a signal on send's parameters, at which point the vocabulary gains abandoned and the contract gains the case that a withdrawal is not reported as a refusal.

premises.owed: DispatchNamespaceLike models a Workers for Platforms namespace as one get(scriptName, parameters) that answers a Fetcher, answers nothing, or throws. A real dispatch namespace is reachable in no local lane. Discharging this needs a Workers for Platforms account, an uploaded tenant script, a dispatch_namespaces binding, and a live-lane run that resolves and fetches through it — including whether a streamed body preserves status, headers and back-pressure without turning into a throw the adapter leaves unclassified.

DispatchFetchServiceScope's disposer is an empty body, which is correct only if a Fetcher from a dispatch namespace holds nothing that must be released. Discharging this needs a live lane that resolves many Fetchers without disposing them and observes whether an RPC session or a subrequest budget leaks. Until then finding SVC-F14 stands.

The adapter validates dispatch parameters and forwards them; nothing local observes that they arrive in the dispatched script's own environment. Discharging this needs a live-lane fetch through a dispatched script that echoes the parameters it received.

premises.declaration: SPEC §14's boundary rule (SPEC.md:2781-2789): a destination the Tenant does not control is outside the trust boundary. A dispatched script or a loaded isolate is authored elsewhere, so nothing it answers is trusted and nothing it throws is attributable to this protocol.

premises.owed: requireAttachmentSize measures the UTF-8 length of the JSON form and the module states the platform measures the structured clone, so the two agree only approximately. Discharging this needs a workerd or live run storing an attachment under the ceiling by JSON measure and over it by clone measure, showing whether the platform refuses on an already-accepted socket — which is precisely the unrepairable state the attach-before-accept ordering exists to prevent.

The structural lane round-trips the attachment through a structured clone in a double. Discharging this needs live evidence for a socket that genuinely hibernated and was revived, comparing the revived attachment to the stored one.

The protocol.invalid-state send refusal is reachable in production only if a real hibernating socket's send throws rather than buffering silently. Discharging this needs a live replay of a payload large enough to exceed the socket's buffer, and the same lane would settle whether the platform accept can fail after a successful attachment write.

The Cap'n Web provider capability plane (packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/provider-capability.ts) is the one external service protocol this artifact does not model: its contract suite was still in flight when the artifact was frozen. Until it lands, invocation.invalid — the undisclosed code that boundary collapses every unrecognised failure to — is accounted as outside the taxonomy rather than mapped by a service that does not answer it. Discharging this means adding the service with its own operation, reply and refusal vocabularies (authenticate as the only method an unauthenticated peer can reach, the handshake that must answer 101 with a socket, per-call re-mediation, and a refusal that cuts the whole session) and its own parameterised suite against a reference and the real Cap'n Web session on workerd.

premises.owed: The measurement that a callee-side AgentCoreError arrives with its name and code intact was taken through vitest-pool-workers' Durable Object stub wrapper, not through a deployed Worker-to-Durable-Object stub. The live suite files are in the frozen fingerprint set, so this needs a consented live re-run rather than an edit.

The idempotency case runs inside one Tenant isolate lifetime. Discharging this needs an eviction between the two deliveries, so the second is answered from the Tenant's durable record rather than from a live guard. citedElsewhere.statement: Every durable read and write in packages/agent-core-cloudflare goes through CloudflareSqlite inside storage.transactionSync; the substrate contracts model it as the store seam with its own laws, adapters and premises. Restating it here would give one seam two contracts that could disagree.

The single physical alarm slot, its claim arbitration and its fenced release are the alarm seam's laws. Reconciliation, resumable operations and permit retention all ride that one alarm rather than any external scheduler, so they inherit the seam's contract.

R2 is reached only through R2ContentObjectRepository and R2ContentStore, whose content-addressing, digest verification, tenant-scoped keys and buffered bound are the content seam's laws and finding SC-F3's disposition. The environment and slate providers use the same injected repository.

The queue disposition protocol — independent per-message dispositions, an undecodable body retried rather than acknowledged, dead-letter custody by configuration — is the queue seam's law set. No queue producer call exists anywhere in src, so only the consumer side has a protocol to model.

Dynamic Worker Loader loads — for authored code, for hosted facets and for the dynamic half of a deployment — are the isolate seam: a required compute bound, a fresh isolate per submission, no ambient egress, and reach limited to the passed capabilities.

Namespace lookup, fresh-stub retry and stub-failure classification are the rpc seam. The tenant.authority service modelled here rides that transport and adds its own request and reply vocabulary on top of it; the transport's own laws are not restated.

There is no HTTP ingress protocol in these packages to model. createCloudflareWorker forwards fetch(request, environment, context) verbatim to a host-supplied AuthoritativeWorkerRouter and delegates queue(batch) to the queue seam; the Durable Object entrypoint delegates fetch, alarm, webSocketMessage, webSocketClose and webSocketError to a host-supplied serving object once its schema and startup admission clear. Zero `new Response(` constructors exist anywhere in the three src trees, so routes, status codes and bodies are entirely the composition root's. The one inbound protocol these packages do own is the hibernating view stream, modelled here as view.stream, and the one admission rule they own is the provider capability handshake, modelled here as part of provider.capability.

The device facet declares an outbound transport port with no implementation anywhere in src, exactly as the web facet does. It is recorded rather than modelled because it has neither a bound adapter nor a reference implementation nor a §13 atom of its own to anchor a taxonomy; inventing one would be inventing a contract for a service this repository does not call. The web.egress contract states the shape both share, and premise webEgressHasNoBoundAdapter states what an unbound port owes.

findings.statement: A credential resolution failure has no code. `send` resolves the credential before the try block deliberately, so it is not misreported as an unreachable endpoint — but nothing then classifies it, and whatever the host's closure threw escapes `complete()` as itself. A caller reading codes cannot distinguish a credential outage from a broken adapter, and no retry policy can key on it.
findings.modelled: The reply vocabulary answers it as `indeterminate` carrying the cause, which is the honest reading rather than a refusal the service never gave. The contract pins it at test/model-service.test.ts#model inference service protocol leaves a credential resolution failure outside the taxonomy entirely. Closing it would mean adding a `model.credential-unavailable` code to HarnessErrorCode, which is a taxonomy change and not this lane's to make unilaterally.

findings.statement: A malformed provider reply can escape the `model.malformed-response` taxonomy as a raw TypeError. `readToolCalls` narrows the tool name to a string and then hands it to `new BindingName(name)`, whose TextId constructor refuses an empty or over-long value with a TypeError. A reply carrying `function.name: ""` therefore passes every check the reader makes and throws a platform error type out of the adapter.
findings.modelled: The contract's `faults` scenario drives exactly this reply for the real adapter and observes `indeterminate`, so the hole is measured rather than assumed. The fix is one line in `readToolCalls` — refuse an unconstructable binding name as `model.malformed-response` — but it is an adapter behaviour change and this lane models rather than repairs.

findings.statement: The inventory behind this artifact found exactly one network egress in all three packages' src trees: the model provider's fetch. Verified absent everywhere in src: the Workers AI binding (env.AI), Vectorize, KV, D1, Hyperdrive, Browser Rendering, Email, Analytics Engine, Workflows, Containers, Cron Triggers, the Cache API, HTMLRewriter, the Queues producer API, the Durable Object native key/value storage API, a Secrets Store binding, and any generic service binding beyond the three shapes already modelled (Durable Object stub, dispatch-namespace Fetcher, Worker Loader entrypoint). No contract is written for any of them, because a contract for a service the repository does not call would be a specification with no subject.

findings.statement: The idempotency obligation and the redirect loop are in direct tension, and the contract now executes it. WebBackend.fetch re-sends every hop under ONE EffectDispatch, while WebTransport's docstring tells the provider to treat dispatch.idempotencyKey as THE dedup key. A provider that does exactly that answers hop two from its own ledger with hop one's redirect, and the chain dies with redirect.denied while the provider is holding the answer the caller asked for. The protocol offers the provider no hop discriminator at all, which is why both contract references had to mix the hop's requested URL into their ledger key — a discriminator the protocol does not declare.
findings.code: packages/agent-core/src/facets/web/facet.ts#WebBackend.fetch re-uses one dispatch across the hop loop; #WebTransport states the key obligation
findings.modelled: Executed at test/profiles/facets/web-egress-service.test.ts#web egress service protocol cannot follow a redirect when the provider dedups on the idempotency key alone. Any real adapter meets it on its first redirect. Closing it means declaring a per-hop discriminator in WebTransportRequest, which is a SPEC §11 change rather than this lane's.

findings.statement: One kernel code carries seven detail codes and eleven refusal positions. WebPolicyError passes operation.invalid-input to AgentCoreError for every WebPolicyErrorCode, so a caller outside the facet that catches AgentCoreError and switches on code cannot distinguish an SSRF refusal from a malformed cache key. Only detailCode separates them, and that field lives on DetailedProfileError rather than in the kernel error vocabulary.
findings.modelled: The reply vocabulary carries both levels on every refusal, and WebPolicyErrorCode rather than AgentCoreErrorCode is the accountable union for this service, so the taxonomy is complete at the level that actually distinguishes.

The facet has no bound transport and four of its five policy ports have no implementation, so "verified" for the WEB family currently means the policy chain behaves given collaborators nobody has written. That is a true statement about the policy chain and not a statement about egress.

findings.statement: WebBackend.search declares Promise<WebResponse> and raises search.invalid synchronously: both refusals precede the first awaitable call, so `backend.search(...).catch(handler)` never sees two of the seven refusals — the throw escapes at the call site instead. readCached is synchronous throughout. The facade happens to be safe because the runtime wraps the handler, but the backend's own surface is a mixed synchronous and asynchronous throw.
findings.modelled: The contract's reply function invokes inside the try, so it observes both forms identically; that is a property of the contract rather than of the seam, and it is recorded here rather than presented as the seam being uniform.

findings.statement: CREDENTIAL_HEADERS is a module-private `new Set([...])` — a static string-keyed membership table, which this repository's own rule says must be a Readonly<Record<string, true>> — and it is not exported. No test can assert over it, so the contract restates the three header names and a drift between the two lists is undetectable. The facet's existing test covers authorization and cookie but never proxy-authorization; the contract covers all three at two casings each.

findings.modelled: Restated in the contract body with a comment saying it is a restatement. Exporting the table would let the contract assert over the real one; that is a one-line source change and this lane models rather than repairs.

findings.statement: FixedWindowRatePolicy defaults its clock to the ambient one. In a repository whose rule is that every clock is injected, the default makes an un-injected rate policy silently time-dependent: tests always pass a clock, and production code that forgot to would not fail anywhere.
findings.modelled: Out of the reply vocabulary entirely — a rate policy's clock is not a protocol value. Recorded because the rate invariant this contract asserts is only as good as the clock the policy reads.

findings.statement: WebPolicyError is publicly exported and the backend never wraps what its collaborators throw, so an untrusted transport or policy can forge ANY refusal in the taxonomy — including url.denied — indistinguishably from a backend decision. The facet's own existing DedupWebTransport does exactly this: it signals a crash after send by throwing WebPolicyError("url.denied"), which under this taxonomy classifies a provider crash as a URL-policy refusal.
findings.code: packages/agent-core/src/facets/web/facet.ts#WebPolicyError is exported; #WebBackend.fetch calls transport.send and the policy ports without wrapping what they throw
findings.modelled: The contract's references throw a TypeError for a crash so its indeterminate case stays honest, and the artifact states plainly that the reply function structurally cannot tell a backend-raised refusal from a transport-forged one. No provenance check was invented, because the protocol offers none.

findings.statement: A redirect re-sends the caller's method and body unchanged to the redirect target, and WebTransportResponse carries a redirect location with no status, so 301, 302, 303, 307 and 308 are indistinguishable at the seam. A POST body therefore follows a redirect chosen by the first host to a second host, and the 303 downgrade to GET that a normal HTTP client performs cannot be expressed. The credential policy is re-consulted per hop; the body is not re-authorized in any sense.
findings.code: packages/agent-core/src/facets/web/facet.ts#WebTransportResponse carries redirect without a status; #WebBackend.fetch re-sends request.method and the buffered body on the next hop
findings.modelled: Recorded on the redirect invariant as the half that is not honored and not expressible at this seam, rather than left inside a verdict of honored.

findings.statement: The stub-shape guard is vacuous across the boundary it exists to guard. requireCapability proves each of the three operations exists with an in-check plus a callable check, but on a real RPC stub every property access is a lazily resolved RPC method — so a Durable Object stub for an object implementing NONE of the operations constructs all three transports without a refusal. The failure surfaces later, at the call, as a platform TypeError with no code, which the contract must answer as indeterminate rather than operation.invalid-output. The check is meaningful only for a malformed local object.
findings.modelled: Recorded as a refuted invariant rather than a scoped pass, and driven on workerd at cloudflare/test/cloudflare/authority-service.test.ts#Tenant authority service protocol on workerd admits a stub whose receiver implements none of the operations and faults at the call. Closing it would mean probing each operation with a call rather than a property read, which changes when the transport speaks to the Tenant and is not this lane's to decide.

findings.statement: A callee-side refusal loses its class but keeps its code. Measured on workerd through the pool's Durable Object stub: an AgentCoreError raised inside the Tenant object arrives at the caller with own properties stack, message, name, code and remote, and instanceof AgentCoreError is false. Every classifier or assertion in this repository written as an instanceof AgentCoreError check therefore cannot hold across this boundary — which is why the package's existing cross-object permit test asserts on messages instead of codes.
findings.code: packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/permit-transport.ts and packages/agent-core-cloudflare/test/assertions.ts, whose expectOperationalFailure is an instanceof assertion
findings.modelled: The contract's classifier reads name and code, so one body classifies correctly in both lanes, and the artifact states the boundary rule rather than leaving it to be rediscovered. The repo-wide consequence for the instanceof-based assertion helpers is reported, not repaired.

findings.statement: Redelivery forwarding is an unbounded re-charge at the Tenant. Two deliveries of one claim reach the Tenant twice by design — the capability is a guard, not a cache — and rely on the Tenant's issuer replaying rather than re-deciding. Nothing bounds how many times ONE admitted key may be redelivered: MAXIMUM_KEYED_CALLS bounds distinct keys only. A holder of one capability can therefore make its Tenant repeat the issuance lookup arbitrarily often under a single admitted key, inside the Tenant's own I/O context.
findings.code: packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/permit-capability.ts#TargetBoundTenantAuthority admits a matching repeat and forwards it, with MAXIMUM_KEYED_CALLS bounding only the number of distinct keys
findings.modelled: The idempotency invariant states plainly that the one effect is the Tenant's durable decision and not the arrival count, so the artifact does not claim a per-key delivery bound that does not exist.

findings.statement: Disclosure at this seam is total, and the sibling provider capability seam makes the opposite choice without either of them saying so. A Tenant refusal crosses with its verbatim message and a stack own property; the messages disclose the exported key-length, key-count and blob bounds and the holder's own idempotency key, all of which are public or holder-supplied, but the stack is a Tenant-internal detail reaching a target Actor. The provider capability boundary deliberately collapses a provider-internal failure to a code with no stack and no cause. Nothing in either transport records that this seam does not collapse.
findings.code: packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/permit-transport.ts and packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/permit-capability.ts raise through the shared error port without rewriting; packages/agent-core-cloudflare/src/provider-capability.ts declares a closed disclosure set and strips the stack
findings.modelled: Recorded rather than repaired: which of the two policies is right is a SPEC §10.3 question. The measurement is that stack is present as an own property on the delivered value; whether its frames are the callee's was not measured.

findings.statement: The caller's own release of a capability is indistinguishable from a fault. After the holder disposes the stub, a further call throws a platform error with no code, so the contract answers indeterminate; the callee-side equivalent is a refusal with authority.denied. The same prose failure — the capability is gone — lands in two reply kinds depending on which side released it. A distinct withdrawn kind would separate a caller's own withdrawal from a genuine unknown, exactly as model.inference separates abandoned from indeterminate.

findings.modelled: Left as indeterminate rather than invented as a fifth kind, because a reply vocabulary is a protocol change and this artifact's own model.inference precedent shows what the fix looks like when it is made deliberately.

findings.statement: The callee's empty-nonce and empty-digest refusal is unreachable through the caller-half transport: the records transport always passes a 64-character hex digest and a nonce that came from a claim. The branch is reachable only by a holder calling the capability object directly. Recorded so the artifact does not claim the transport can produce a refusal it cannot.
